newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Gulf War compensation body welcomes Iraqi oil flow.
newsitem.headline: Gulf War compensation body welcomes Iraqi oil flow.

text.p: The U.N. Compensation Commission welcomed resumption of the flow of Iraqi oil on Tuesday, saying its 30 per cent share of revenues should enable it to begin paying substantial reparations to Gulf War victims by March.

The cash-strapped U.N. body said it hoped to make initial partial payments totalling $140 million to 56,000 individuals either forced to leave Kuwait or Iraq or who had incurred personal financial loss.

But Western diplomats said that the $100 million a month coming into the fund's coffers under the limited oil-for-food deal would hardly begin to make a dent in $200 billion in outstanding claims against Baghdad.

The Geneva-based fund, set up by the Security Council to compensate direct losses caused by Iraq's invasion and occupation of Kuwait from August 1990 to January 1991, is trying to implement the largest compensation programme ever.

Under the terms of resolution 986, 30 per cent of the $2 billion in oil sales over six months would go to the Commission, which is processing huge claims from individuals, corporations and governments.
This would translate into $100 million a month under the oil-for-food deal, which is renewable for another six months.
Carlos Alzamora, a former Peruvian diplomat who is executive secretary of the commission, welcomed implementation of the deal, under which food and medicine will be bought for Iraqis.

"Finally we are able to provide relief to the Iraqi people and innocent victims of the invasion. It took too long, but as we say in Spanish, it is never too late when joy arrives," Alzamora told Reuters.

"We are ready to start paying at the rhythm of resources made available to us. We are ready to start the biggest compensation programme in history with the first substantial payments to claimants," he added.
A U.N. source said: "We could see money come in the latter part of January...We could be paying out by early March."
The commission will have approved nearly $7 billion in awards to claimants by year-end, but had a meager $10 million in its coffers to last through April.

To date, it has only been able to pay out $13.4 million in awards to 4,000 priority claimants for death of a close relative or serious personal injury. This represents full payment of all claims in this humanitarian category.
Under rules set by the Governing Council, composed of the 15 members of the Security Council, payments are to proceed according to the order in which the claims were approved.
The first partial payments will be to 53,000 claimants forced to flee, for a total of $134.6 million, as well as nearly 3,000 claimants who filed for financial loss of up to $100,000.
Given financial constraints, under a Governing Council decision, claimants will receive $2,500 of their claim for now.

At its next regular meeting on Monday, the Governing Council will consider the still-secret decision of a neutral arbitration panel which weighed the $961 million claim by the Kuwait Oil Company for damages and costs related to extinguishing the oil well fires allegedly set by departing Iraqi forces.

The commission's funds so far have come from government donations and seized Iraqi assets. Its 120 staff have been demoralised by the perpetual funding uncertainty and their short-term contracts, according to U.N. sources.
A Western diplomat told Reuters: "We are pleased that implementation is beginning and we look forward to funds coming in. It is good for the UNCC and for the people with claims.
"But given the size of the claims it won't put a dent in the immediate future," he added.
